content: Basil, scientifically known as Ocimum basilicum, belongs to the family Lamiaceae. It is a tender, low-growing herb that thrives as a perennial in warm, tropical climates. Basil is native to India and other tropical regions of Asia, where it has been cultivated for over 5,000 years. There are numerous varieties of basil, with sweet basil being the type most commonly used in Italian cuisine, while Thai basil and holy basil are more prevalent in Asian cooking. Basil is a key ingredient in Italian dishes and plays a significant role in the cuisines of Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos. Its flowers are relatively large, white, and arranged in terminal spikes. Unlike most members of the Lamiaceae family, basil’s four stamens and pistil are not tucked under the upper lip of the corolla but instead rest over the inferior portion. After pollination by insects, the corolla falls off, and four round achenes develop within the bilabiate calyx. Basil has a flavor reminiscent of anise, with a strong, sweet, and pungent aroma. It is highly sensitive to cold and grows best in hot, dry conditions. While most basil varieties are treated as annuals, some, such as African Blue and Holy Thai basil, are perennials. The name basil is derived from the Greek word βασιλεύς (basileus), meaning king, as it is believed to have grown at the site where St. Constantine and Helen discovered the Holy Cross. The Oxford English Dictionary suggests that basil may have been used in royal ointments, baths, or medicines. It is still referred to as the king of herbs by many culinary experts. An alternative etymology links the name to the Latin word basilicus, meaning dragon, which is also the root of the word basilisk, though this is likely a reinterpretation of the Greek origin. Culinary Use Basil is best used fresh, as cooking can quickly destroy its flavor. In recipes, it is typically added at the last moment to preserve its aromatic qualities. Fresh basil can be stored briefly in plastic bags in the refrigerator or for longer periods in the freezer after being blanched in boiling water. Dried basil, however, loses much of its flavor, and what remains has a weak, hay-like taste due to coumarin. Basil is a primary ingredient in pesto, a green Italian sauce made with olive oil and pine nuts, originating from Genoa. Popular Mediterranean basil cultivars include Genovese, Purple Ruffles, Mammoth, Cinnamon, Lemon, Globe, and African Blue. In Chinese cuisine, both fresh and dried basil are used in soups and other dishes. In Taiwan, fresh basil leaves are added to thick soups and served with fried chicken. Basil is also paired with fresh fruits, particularly strawberries, raspberries, and dark plums, in jams and sauces. Vietnamese flat-leaf basil, which has a slightly different flavor, is often considered more suitable for use with fruits. Basil Seeds The seeds of certain basil varieties become gelatinous when soaked in water and are used in Asian beverages and desserts, such as falooda and sherbet. These seeds, known by various names such as sabja, tukmaria, or hột é, are valued for their medicinal properties in Ayurveda, the traditional medical system of India. Other Basil Varieties Several other basil species, including those from the Ocimum genus, are cultivated across Asia. Asian basils often have a clove-like flavor that is stronger than Mediterranean varieties. Holy basil, or tulsi, is a sacred plant in India. In China, local basil cultivars are called 九層塔 (jiǔ-kéng-tǎ, meaning nine-level pagoda), while imported varieties are referred to as 羅勒 (luó-lè) or 巴西里 (bā-xī-lǐ), though the latter term may also refer to parsley. Lemon basil, which contains the chemical citral, has a distinct lemony aroma and flavor. It is widely used in Indonesia, where it is called kemangi and served raw alongside vegetables as an accompaniment to fried fish or duck. Its flowers, when broken up, are used as a zesty salad condiment. Chemical Components The diverse scents of basil varieties are due to the presence of different essential oils in varying proportions. Sweet basil’s clove-like aroma comes from eugenol, the same compound found in cloves. Lemon and lime basils owe their citrus scent to higher levels of citral and limonene, the latter being the compound responsible for the scent of lemon peel. African Blue basil has a strong camphor aroma due to elevated levels of camphor and camphene. Licorice basil contains anethole, the compound that gives anise its licorice-like scent. Other chemicals contributing to basil’s distinctive aromas include cinnamate (found in cinnamon), citronellol (found in geraniums and roses), geraniol (also in geraniums), linalool (a floral scent found in coriander), methyl chavicol (responsible for tarragon’s aroma), myrcene (found in bay leaves), pinene (responsible for pine oil’s scent), ocimene, and terpineol. Cultivation Basil thrives in warm weather but behaves as an annual in regions prone to frost. In colder climates, such as Northern Europe, northern U.S. states, and New Zealand’s South Island, basil is best started indoors in peat pots and transplanted outdoors in late spring or early summer. It grows well in well-drained, sunny locations. While basil prefers outdoor conditions, it can also be grown indoors in pots, ideally on a windowsill with ample sunlight. It should be protected from cold drafts and thrives in strong sunlight, making greenhouses or row covers ideal. Basil can even be grown under fluorescent lights in basements. Yellowing leaves at the base of the plant indicate insufficient sunlight or over-fertilization. In sunnier climates, such as Southern Europe, southern U.S. states, and New Zealand’s North Island, basil thrives outdoors. It requires regular watering but less attention compared to cooler climates. Basil can also be propagated from cuttings, with stems placed in water until roots develop. Flowering stems reduce leaf production and essential oil content, so growers often pinch off flower stems to encourage leaf growth. Once the plant flowers, it produces seed pods containing small black seeds that can be harvested for planting the following year. Diseases Basil is susceptible to several plant pathogens that can damage crops and reduce yields. Fusarium wilt, a soilborne fungal disease, can rapidly kill young plants. Seedlings are also vulnerable to Pythium damping-off. Gray mold, caused by Botrytis cinerea, is a common foliar disease that can also infect basil post-harvest, potentially killing the entire plant. Black spot, caused by fungi of the Colletotrichum genus, can also affect basil foliage. Health Effects Research has highlighted the health benefits of basil’s essential oils, which possess potent antioxidant, anti-aging, anti-cancer, antiviral, and antimicrobial properties. Basil has been shown to reduce platelet aggregation and experimental thrombus formation in mice. In traditional Indian medicine, basil is used as a supplementary treatment for stress, asthma, and diabetes. However, basil contains estragole, a compound that is a known carcinogen and teratogen in rodents. Cultural Significance Basil holds cultural and symbolic significance in various traditions. In France, it is called l'herbe royale (the royal herb). Jewish folklore claims it provides strength during fasting. In modern Italy, basil symbolizes love, while in ancient Greece, it represented hatred. European folklore sometimes associates basil with Satan, while African legends suggest it protects against scorpions. Holy basil, or tulsi, is revered in Hinduism and is also significant in the Greek Orthodox Church, where it is used to prepare holy water. In India, it is placed in the mouths of the dying to help them reach God. Ancient Egyptians and Greeks believed basil could open the gates of heaven for the deceased. Basil also features in literature, such as Boccaccio’s Decameron and John Keats’ poem Isabella or The Pot of Basil.
